notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Acts 14. They come only from the pages I was able to read, and the URL follows each point.

**Gaps:** I reached my tool limit before I could read netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, catholic.com, any Lutheran site (lcms.org, 1517.org) or any Wesleyan site (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com). I also only saw search-result extracts of Chrysostom's Homily 31 and Preceptaustin, not the full pages. As a result I found nothing usable for v. 24–25 or v. 28, so those verses are left out.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul and Barnabas had just been thrown out of Pisidian Antioch, but they began in the synagogue again. They presented the gospel in a way that invited belief, encouraging people to trust in who Jesus is and what He had done. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Chrysostom (Church Father, honoured by both Catholics and Orthodox): the apostles had not become more timid. He thinks it likely they spoke in a way suited to Greeks too. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210130.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Luke makes clear that not all the Jews of Iconium did this, since many believed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Matthew Henry: the opponents soured and embittered people against both the preachers and the converts. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Chrysostom: "poisoned their minds" means they slandered the apostles and brought endless accusations against them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210130.htm

**v. 3**
- Henry: the more spite they saw against the new converts, the more determined they were to stay, strengthen them and comfort them. He calls the gospel a message of grace: God's goodwill toward us and his means of working in us. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Clarke: no apostle could work a miracle by himself; each needed a special grant from God. (This is in the full page text.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- **Where traditions differ: are signs and wonders for today?** One page shows both sides:
  - Stedman says God's confirming the word with signs is always present when the true gospel is preached.
  - Preceptaustin's own comment gives the cessationist view (that miraculous gifts ended with the apostles): there was no completed Bible yet, so God gave signs to back up the apostles' ministry, and these would fade as Scripture was completed.
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary
- Chrysostom: "bore witness" does not lower the Lord's majesty. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210130.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: this is the first time Acts calls Paul and Barnabas "apostles". The only other time is v. 14. (Full page text.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/

**v. 5**
- Constable: this looks like mob violence rather than a formal Jewish execution. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary
- Henry: once they had the rulers on their side, the plan was to disgrace the apostles and then stone them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Preceptaustin: God is sovereign even over persecution, and he used it to move the missionaries on to Lystra. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary

**v. 6**
- Chrysostom: they did not wait to be attacked. They saw what was intended and fled, never stirring up anger themselves. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210130.htm
- Guzik: William Ramsay showed that Lystra and Derbe were grouped together in Lycaonia only from about AD 37 to 72, the very period of these events. That accuracy helped persuade Ramsay that Acts is reliable. (Full page text.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- A historical point: Preceptaustin notes that later Roman writers such as Cicero placed Iconium in Lycaonia too, which seems to contradict this verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary

**v. 7**
- Toussaint: the verb form stresses that they kept preaching over a period of time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary

**v. 8**
- Guzik, quoting Boice: the apostles preached first and did miracles second, not the other way round. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- GotQuestions: Lystra may have been the first city where they preached straight to Gentiles without starting in a synagogue. https://www.gotquestions.org/Lystra-in-the-Bible.html

**v. 9: "faith to be healed"** (the main verse where views differ)
- Clarke (Methodist): the man got this faith by hearing Paul preach, and believed Jesus could heal him if He chose. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-9.html
- Constable: he believed God could heal him, not that God would. Being sure God would heal him is not what made him well. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-9.html
- Ellicott (Anglican): faith is assumed here as the general, though not universal, condition for miracles. https://biblehub.com/acts/14-9.htm
- How Paul saw the faith:
  - Guzik thinks God probably gave Paul the gift of discernment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
  - Gill says it could have been from the man's looks, gestures, attentive listening, something he said, or revelation. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/acts/14-9.html
  - Bengel calls it "passive faith" with regard to the miracle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-9.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) preached a sermon on this verse and applies it to saving faith: there is such a thing as faith to be saved. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-9.html
- **Debated popular teaching (faith healing):** The "Contending for the Faith" commentary criticises modern "faith healers" who, when healing fails, blame the sick person's lack of faith. It argues the healer is the one who must have faith, not the person being healed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-9.html
- The Greek word for "healed" is often translated "saved", and some commentators say the physical healing here points to spiritual reality. https://biblehub.com/acts/14-9.htm
- A Catholic Bible translation on New Advent renders this "seeing that there was saving faith in him". https://www.newadvent.org/bible/act014.htm

**v. 10**
- Chrysostom: the leaping proved the cure was complete. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210130.htm

**v. 11**
- Guzik: they saw a huge miracle, yet their idea of who God is had not changed. The miracle itself saved no one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Bruce: because the crowd spoke Lycaonian, Paul and Barnabas did not realise what was going on until the preparations were well advanced. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- MacLaren: their cry was a wistful admission of need. "The Word became flesh" is the answer to that need. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-12.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: the crowd saw eloquence in Paul, and eloquence was the special mark of Hermes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-12.htm
- MacLaren: Barnabas was older, and his silence suggested greater dignity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-12.htm
- Local legend: people around Lystra told how Zeus and Hermes once came in disguise, and only an old couple, Philemon and Baucis, took them in. (Barclay) https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-12.html
- Archaeology versus critics. One Bible Hub article cites inscriptions and altars to Zeus and Hermes in the area as support. https://biblehub.com/q/Acts_14_12_and_Lystra_s_culture.htm Another notes that critics point out no record outside the Bible says Barnabas was called Zeus or Paul Hermes. https://biblehub.com/q/why_do_acts_14_11-13_lack_external_proof.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the phrase probably means the temple of Zeus stood at the city entrance, as shrine of its protecting god. The "gates" may be those of the courtyard of the house where the apostles were staying, and oxen were the proper sacrifice for both Zeus and Hermes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-13.html

**v. 14**
- Guzik: tearing their clothes showed they were only human, and was a reaction to blasphemy, not just embarrassment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Chrysostom: they first checked the crowd by what it could see, tearing their garments. Nothing less would have stopped it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210131.htm
- Chrysostom elsewhere asks why the apostles refused worship when Daniel did not. His answer: the Lystrans really thought they were gods. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240226.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: Jesus could not simply be added to their pagan ways. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Henry: God's truth does not need man's lie. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Chrysostom: they not only overturn falsehood but teach truth, saying nothing about invisible things, only about the Creator of what can be seen. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210131.htm
- MacLaren: Paul shaped his style to his audience. Unlike at Athens, there are no poets or arguments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-12.htm

**v. 16**
- Henry: God's patience should lead us to repentance, not make us presume on it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Preceptaustin sees here both God's permission and man's own wilful choice, i.e. God's sovereignty and human free will. Stedman reads it as God gave them free will. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary

**v. 17**
- Guzik: rain and harvests are God's kindness to everyone, which theologians sometimes call common grace. Paul used natural revelation, not Old Testament quotations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Henry: besides conscience within them, the Gentiles had witnesses for God all around them in the bounty of common providence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Ellicott: to peasants the apostles built on a simple natural theology, appealing to God's goodness in nature. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts.html
- Chrysostom: "He did good" quietly accuses them, because having enjoyed such benefits, they had not acknowledged Him. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210131.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: even so, they had great difficulty correcting the Lystrans' wrong ideas of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Henry: idolatry starts when people stop at the human instruments of their blessing and do not look through them to the Author. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm

**v. 19**
- Guzik: this shows how fickle a crowd can be, and it is dangerous for a spiritual leader to allow hero-worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- MacLaren: grammatically it was the Jews who stoned Paul, probably helped by the mob. Did Paul remember Stephen? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-12.htm
- Chrysostom counts Paul's chains and the stoning as glorious for Christ. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230108.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik: Paul was miraculously preserved. Some think he actually died and was raised. Linking it to the vision in 2 Corinthians 12 is possible, but only conjecture. Timothy may have seen it happen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Chrysostom: they went back in so the disciples would not lose heart. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210131.htm

**v. 21**
- Chrysostom: they went on to Derbe and later returned, giving way while passions were roused, then coming back once they had cooled. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210131.htm
- Guzik: the work went on, preaching and making disciples. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/

**v. 22: perseverance and hardship**
- Guzik: Paul could preach this message because he had lived it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
- Henry: people surrounded by temptations to fall away need constant urging to persevere. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- **Reformed and Baptist reading:** Preceptaustin calls this the doctrine of the final perseverance of the saints, treating continuing in faith as proof that faith is genuine, and adds there is no hint that anyone earns salvation by endurance. MacArthur (on a parallel "if") says such warnings target faith that never saved, not a real danger of losing salvation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary
- Toussaint: Paul was not teaching that you must suffer to reach heaven. He meant that the saved would suffer because of their faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary
- I found no Wesleyan or Arminian source on this verse.
- **Against prosperity teaching:** a writer quoted on Preceptaustin says Christianity survives only if we reject any "gospel" that promises glory without suffering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-14-commentary

**v. 23: how elders were "appointed"** (the clearest split between traditions)
- **What the word means.** The Greek word (*cheirotoneō*) originally meant to vote by raising hands.
  - The Pulpit Commentary says that since it describes what Paul and Barnabas did, it cannot possibly mean a vote by the people, and there is no reference to laying on of hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-23.htm
  - Vine: the word means elders were recognised because they were already showing they were gifted by God for the work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/search/dictionary/viewTopic.cfm?topic=VT0000141
- **Anglican, Ellicott:** the word seems to imply popular election by show of hands. He says the apostles acted with the congregation's consent, and so an implied right of veto, with authority like that of later bishops. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-23.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts.html
- **Reformed, Calvin:** translates "ordained by election" and asks whether Paul and Barnabas did this alone by their own authority, which implies they did not. Pastors were appointed so preaching would be permanent and in daily use. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-23.html
- **Baptist, Gill:** the churches chose by joint votes, lifting up their hands, not laying them on, with the apostles presiding. Barnes similarly thinks the apostles presided at the meeting where the choice was made. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-23.htm and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/acts/14-23.html
- **Baptist, MacArthur (gty.org):** reading this as a congregational vote forces the word. Only Barnabas and Paul did the choosing, though the congregation's agreement may be implied. He sees a plurality of elders as the clear New Testament pattern. https://www.gty.org/library/articles/451016/answering-the-key-questions-about-elders
- **Methodist, Clarke:** the people chose by raising hands, and the church's leaders then appointed by laying on hands. Both may have been considered necessary. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-23.html
- **Pentecostal, Assemblies of God:** the congregations may well have had a part in the choice, as with the seven in Acts 6. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Ordination
- **Brethren, Kelly:** "ordained" is misleading. The meaning is "they chose them elders." He rejects both the Church Fathers' reading of laying on of hands and the idea of a congregational vote. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-23.html
- **Themelios (TGC):** Everett Ferguson infers that hands were laid on from the phrase "committing them to the Lord", although the text does not say so. *Cheirotoneō* only later became the church's technical term for "ordain". https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/ordination/
- **Catholic and Orthodox angle:** Chrysostom, commenting on a similar word in Acts 6, says a man lays on his hand but the whole work is God's, and His hand touches the one ordained. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/210114.htm
- On "entrusted them to the Lord": Barnes says they were weak and exposed to danger, but safe in His hands. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/14-23.htm

**v. 26**
- Kelly: v. 26 explains why hands were laid on Barnabas and Saul in Acts 13. It was commending them to God's grace for the work, not giving them authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/14-23.html

**v. 27**
- Henry: God's grace can work without ministers' preaching, but preaching can do nothing without God's grace. Also: the only way into Christ's kingdom is through the door of faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_014.cfm
- Guzik: they reported back to the church that sent them on how God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-14/
